name: Yoba
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Ross, Malcolm. 1988. Proto Oceanic and the Austronesian languages of western Melanesia. Pacific Linguistics C-98. Canberra: ANU.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online: WID Offsite Storage PL6201.R67 1988 (also: archive.org controlled lending)
sources.note: Yoba on pp. 190, 192-195, 205: Central Papuan consonant correspondences (Table 30, Yoba row) and grammatical notes (Magori and Yoba lack postpositions); source list gives 'Yoba: Dutton 1976, n.d.'. No synchronic prosody, no stress.
Only descriptive ref: Dutton 1976, MED 'wordlist_or_less'; no other refs.

sources.citation: OLAC: resources in and about the Yoba language (Wayback capture 2026-01-26)
sources.note: Only primary resource: PARADISEC TD1-P120 'Magore Survey' (Dutton 1972, audio). No language description listed.

sources.citation: Lynch, John, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley. 2002. The Oceanic languages. Richmond: Curzon.
sources.note: Yoba only listed among moribund languages (p. 12, 'fewer than ten speakers at the last recording') and in the language index citing Dutton 1976; no sketch, no phonology.

sources.citation: Ross, M.D. 1994. Central Papuan culture history: some lexical evidence. In A.K. Pawley & M.D. Ross (eds), Austronesian terminologies: continuity and change, 389-479. Pacific Linguistics C-127.
sources.note: Historical-lexical paper. p. 400: 'Magori, Yoba and Bina have very similar phonological histories, and share the rather unusual backing of PCP *r... to Magori k, Yoba and Bina ''.' Appendix 2 consonant-correspondence table has a Yoba row (segmental only); the key symbol '/U in an unstressed syllable' is applied only to North Papuan Mainland rows (Gapapaiwa, Wedau, Tawala, Gumawana, Dobu), never to Yoba. No Yoba stress statement.

sources.citation: Dutton, T. 1982. Borrowing in Austronesian and non-Austronesian languages of coastal south-east mainland Papua New Guinea. In Halim, Carrington & Wurm (eds), Papers from TICAL vol. 1: Currents in Oceanic, 109-177. Pacific Linguistics C-74.
sources.note: Sec. 2.2 pp. 112-113 on the four Oumic remnants; p. 116: 'Bina, Yoba and Ouma are the least reliably recorded (and in that order) because they are moribund'. Appendix 3 'Ouma and Magori sound systems' does not cover Yoba. Yoba only a comparandum (YOB) in wordlists. No stress statement.

sources.citation: Dutton, T.E. 1976. Austronesian languages: eastern part of south-eastern mainland Papua. In Wurm (ed.), NGAL vol. 2, 321-333. PL C-39. DOI 10.15144/PL-C39.321
sources.note: Survey only: Yoba 'formerly spoken inland of Magori along the middle-Bailebo River but is now only remembered by two speakers, a man, Aruba Inabe, and his mother, Bo'odi, at present living in Laua village' (pp. 326-327); cognate percentages; no phonology, no stress.

sources.citation: Dutton, T.E. 1976. Magori and similar languages of south-east Papua. In S.A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 2: Austronesian languages, 581-636. Pacific Linguistics C-39. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-C39.581
sources.note: Sec. 4.5.2.6.1 'Phonological evidence' p. 594 (page image checked) treats Ouma, Magori, Yoba and Bina jointly: five vowels, consonants p t k ' b d g m n v r, allophony, 'All syllables are open and there are no consonant clusters.' Nothing on stress/accent/tone. Yoba wordlist column in Table 2 (pp. 610-618; p. 614 image checked) printed without stress marks (apostrophe = glottal stop). Materials were ~270-item TRIPP wordlists plus some elicited grammar (p. 593).
Stub citing Ethnologue 25 only; notes PARADISEC TD1 holds Yoba materials; no phonology.

sources.citation: Dutton, Tom (collector). 1972. Magore Survey. PARADISEC TD1-P120 (audio, 1h34): 'Aruba (of Lawa Village) with Yoba grammatical material [015-147]'
